items.title: `intent://` in a WebView — the vector that upgrades every receiver primitive to one click
items.severity_note: High (the item is a *vector*; it inherits the ceiling of whatever component it reaches — up to Critical through D05-051 or D05-029)
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies) — rated on the component reached
items.attacker: AM-02 (remote, one click) — this item exists to *change the attacker model* of the rest of the chapter from AM-03
items.applies_to: Any app whose WebView (or any `shouldOverrideUrlLoading` / deep-link router) calls `Intent.parseUri()` on attacker-reachable content. Also reachable from an XSS in any page the WebView loads.
items.maps_to: Oversecured WebView checklist ("arbitrary activity launching via the `intent://` scheme"); CWE-926; `developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/risks/intent-redirection`
items.test:
The parser defect is owned by D10-065 (`shouldOverrideUrlLoading`) and D08-022 (`Intent.parseUri` on
attacker text) — run them first and file it there. The D05-specific question is only: is the parsed Intent
dispatched with `sendBroadcast`/`startService` (reaches the receivers in this chapter directly) or with
`startActivity` (reaches D04)? Record that, and re-state the attacker model on every D05 finding it reaches —
one `parseUri` call site converts the whole chapter from AM-03 to AM-02 (a link on a web page), a full
severity band.
items.how: ```bash grep -rn 'parseUri\|Intent.parseUri\|URI_ALLOW_UNSAFE\|URI_INTENT_SCHEME\|URI_ANDROID_APP_SCHEME' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -B6 -A12 grep -rn 'shouldOverrideUrlLoading' $DEC/jadx/sources/ -A25 | grep -nE 'startActivity|sendBroadcast|startService|parseUri' ``` The vulnerable shape lives in D10-065 / D08-022; the receiver-targeted attacker page: ```html go ``` ```bash adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://zq7x4mk9.collab.example/poc.html" adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -m1 topResumedActivity ```
items.proof:
A component of the target app reacting to a click on a **remote page** — `topResumedActivity`
naming the target, or the receiver's marker-bearing side effect — recorded end to end from the browser,
with no attacker app installed at any point.
items.escalation:
This is a D10 defect used as a delivery vector for D05. File the WebView/parser defect in
D10, then re-state the attacker model on every receiver finding it reaches. `Intent.parseUri(url, 0)` is
bad; `URI_ALLOW_UNSAFE` (flag value 4) is strictly worse because it re-enables the unsafe-parse path —
note which one the app uses (see D08).
items.ruled_out_when:
No `parseUri` call site exists, **or** every call site strips
`Intent.FLAG_GRANT_*`/`setSelector` and constrains the resulting Intent to an allow-listed component
before dispatch (quote the allow-list), **or** the parsed Intent is only ever passed to `startActivity`
and every target activity in this app is already independently reachable and harmless. "The WebView only
loads our own domain" is not a ruled-out entry unless you also tested for reflected content in that
domain.

items.title: `directBootAware="true"` receiver that runs before the device is ever unlocked
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies); chain to `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) when the pre-unlock path exposes a token
items.attacker: AM-03 (an attacker app can declare `directBootAware` on its own components too, so it runs in the same window); AM-10 for the physical-locked variant
items.applies_to: Android 7+ file-based-encryption devices. `android:directBootAware` defaults to **false** on activities, services, receivers and providers; `LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED` is delivered only to direct-boot-aware components. During Direct Boot only **device-protected** storage (`/data/user_de/<user>/<pkg>`) is available.
items.maps_to: `developer.android.com/guide/topics/manifest/receiver-element` (`android:directBootAware`); ATT&CK T1624.001 (`LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED`); MASWE-0018
items.test:
The component census is owned by D03-039; the D05-specific questions are the receiver's two failure modes. A direct-boot-aware receiver executes in a state the rest of the app never designs for: no user
has authenticated, credential-encrypted storage is unavailable, and any check that reads it fails. Two
distinct questions: does the handler **fail open** when its credential-encrypted state is unreadable, and
what does it keep in device-protected storage so that it can work at all?
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'directBootAware="true"' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -n -B2 -A8 'LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml
grep -rn 'createDeviceProtectedStorageContext\|moveSharedPreferencesFrom\|moveDatabaseFrom\|isUserUnlocked' $DEC/jadx/sources/
# reboot and, WITHOUT entering the PIN, drive the receiver
adb reboot && adb wait-for-device
adb shell dumpsys user | grep -i unlocked          # record the pre-unlock state
adb shell am broadcast -n com.target.app/.BootReceiver                       # null action: LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED is protected and refused even with -n (D05-006)
adb shell am broadcast -n com.target.app/.BootReceiver -a com.poc.zq7x4mk9   # unprotected action
adb shell 'ls -la /data/user_de/0/com.target.app 2>/dev/null'
```
items.proof:
The handler running with `dumpsys user` showing the user still locked — and, where it applies,
the contents of `/data/user_de/0/com.target.app/shared_prefs/*.xml` printed from that same pre-unlock
shell. Record `getprop ro.crypto.type` (`file` vs `block`) because the storage split only exists under
FBE.
items.escalation:
→ D11 (what lives in device-protected storage is outside the credential key, so disk
encryption is not the control the vendor thinks it is); → D13 if a token or device-binding secret is
there; pair with D04's `showWhenLocked` items for a complete pre-unlock chain.
items.ruled_out_when:
No component declares `directBootAware="true"` (the default is false, so the grep
returning nothing *is* the negative here), **or** every direct-boot-aware handler gates its work on
`UserManager.isUserUnlocked()` and no secret is written through
`createDeviceProtectedStorageContext()` — quote the gate and list what the `user_de` directory actually
contains.
The explicit-send control: the handler's first statement rejects any action other than the protected one — quote that branch; it is the single control (D05-006).

items.title: Turn the broadcast-harvested route inventory into a shadow-API version diff
items.severity_note: Critical (through the backend, not through the broadcast)
items.vrt: `broken_authentication_and_session_management.authentication_bypass` (P1) where the old version accepts no token; `broken_access_control.idor.*` (P1/P2/P3) where it exposes objects the current version protects; a bare version difference is **Informational**
items.attacker: AM-01 (once it is the backend, no device is involved)
items.applies_to: Any app whose broadcasts, implicit intents or sniffed API-response bus (D05-030, D05-031) reveal backend hosts, routes or an API version segment.
items.maps_to: Shadow/zombie-API methodology from the bug-hunting corpus ("a mobile app's hardcoded backend calls look older than the current web app's"); CWE-1059-adjacent operational debt — file under the behaviour you prove, not under "old version"
items.test:
The broadcast bus is a free route inventory: a request-complete broadcast carries the URL, the
method and often the whole response body for every call the app makes. The structural bet worth making on
every mobile engagement is that those hardcoded routes are an **older API version** than the current web
client uses — with weaker auth, weaker rate limits, weaker input validation and more field exposure. The
version difference is not the finding; the weakened control is.
items.how:
```bash
# routes from the sniffed extras and from the package itself
grep -rohE 'https?://[A-Za-z0-9._-]+(/[A-Za-z0-9._~%-]+)*' /tmp/sniffed_extras.log "$DEC/jadx/sources" \
  | sort -u > /tmp/routes.txt
wc -l /tmp/routes.txt        # count everything; never iterate this in a shell array loop
```
```python
# behavioural diff, same operation, same account, both versions — Python, not a shell loop
import itertools, requests
VERSIONS = ["v1", "v2", "v3", "internal", "legacy"]
OP = "/users/{id}"
for v, tok in itertools.product(VERSIONS, ["", "expired", "lowpriv", "valid"]):
    url = f"https://api.target.example/api/{v}{OP.format(id=1337)}"
    h = {} if not tok else {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKENS[tok]}"}
    r = requests.get(url, headers=h, timeout=10)
    print(v, tok or "none", r.status_code, len(r.content))
```
Diff four behaviours for the **same** operation: auth strength (does the old version accept no token, an
expired token, or a lower-privilege token the current one rejects?), rate limiting (burst both; a missing
429 means throttling was never backported), input validation (the same oversized or injected payload to
both), and field exposure (does the old version return internal ids or PII the current one redacts?).
items.proof:
The same request against both versions side by side, with the same account, showing the
control present on one and absent on the other — and a **body** diff, not a status-code diff. A 200 with a
byte-identical body is not a bypass. Before claiming a reflected or injected value, search the baseline
response for your marker first.
items.escalation:
→ D15 for the filing; the mobile side of the finding is only how you discovered the
route. Where the old version accepts an unauthenticated call, run the layer-ordering check before
claiming auth bypass: a `400 "field X is required"` from an unauthenticated request does not prove you
passed auth, because many stacks run the body parser or sanitiser in front of the auth middleware —
re-test with a minimal well-formed `{}` body.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every version prefix you found answers 404 or connection-refused, **or** the four
behaviours are identical across versions when tested with the same account and the same payloads. Record
the version list you swept and the four-behaviour result table — "only v2 exists" is a defensible
negative; "I only tried v1" is not.

items.title: Prove delivery-order and spray wins statistically, never from one lucky run
items.vrt: n/a — enabler; governs D05-036, D05-037, D05-038, D05-042, D05-043, D05-046 and the D05-051 spray
items.applies_to: Every claim of the form "my receiver gets it first", "my component wins resolution", "the consent-Intent spray lands".
items.maps_to: Statistical-Sample Rule and the Shell-Loop Ban from the bug-hunting corpus
items.test:
Delivery order, resolver ordering and the background-activity-launch spray are all **races**.
One success is an anecdote, and a triager who reproduces once and fails writes the report off. Quantify
the win rate before you claim the primitive, and quantify it again on the device family the client cares
about.
items.how:
Interleave control and test, at least ten trials each, and **count your results** — a zsh array
loop can fail silently and still print a plausible transcript:
```python
import subprocess, collections, random, time
PKG="com.target.app"; ACT="com.target.app.ORDERED_ACTION"
res=collections.Counter()
trials=[("test",)]*10 + [("control",)]*10
random.shuffle(trials)
for (kind,) in trials:
    subprocess.run(["adb","shell","logcat","-c"])
    if kind=="control":
        subprocess.run(["adb","uninstall","com.poc.zeroperm"])
    subprocess.run(["adb","shell","am","broadcast","-a",ACT,"--receiver-foreground"])
    time.sleep(1.5)
    out=subprocess.run(["adb","shell","logcat","-d","-s","PoC","TARGET"],
                       capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
    first = "PoC" if out.find("PoC") != -1 and (out.find("TARGET")==-1 or out.find("PoC")<out.find("TARGET")) else "TARGET"
    res[(kind,first)]+=1
print(res, "trials:", sum(res.values()))   # assert the count equals len(trials)
```
For a timing-shaped claim (who was scheduled first, whether the spray beat the resume), report mean,
median and σ per group and require the difference to be at least 2σ — network and scheduler jitter
routinely produce 2× single-shot outliers.
items.proof:
A table of n trials with the win count and the failure mode named, included in the report. For
the D05-051 spray, state the precondition honestly — "captures on the victim's next OTP screen, observed
in k of n attempts" — rather than "unconditional".
items.escalation:
None — it is what makes D05-036, D05-043 and D05-051 survive triage rather than being
closed as not-reproducible.
items.ruled_out_when:
Across n >= 10 interleaved trials the attacker component never wins, or wins at a
rate indistinguishable from the control. That is a true negative: record the trial count, the win rate
and the device API level, because the same PoC may win on a different release (see the Android 16 gate in
D05-036).

items.title: Run the pre-severity gate against the Critical claim, not against the receiver
items.vrt: n/a — governs every Critical/High filing in this domain
items.applies_to: Every Critical or High claim in D05.
items.maps_to: Pre-severity gate and retraction discipline from the bug-hunting corpus
items.test:
Shared doctrine with D02-070, D04-067, D07-075, D08-065, D09-080 and D13-006; the D05-specific content is the gate list in How. Write the draft Critical title, then substitute the **Critical claim** — not the bug — into each
question. (1) Have I validated the full chain to attacker-attainable impact, or only a primitive in the
middle? "Unguarded receiver confirmed" is not "session stolen". (2) What does the attacker walk away with,
in one concrete sentence? (3) Have I reproduced the full chain end to end at least twice, once during
discovery and once for the PoC? (4) Is there still a gate — a signature check, an audience check, a
handshake identifier, the BAL visible-window constraint — in the way? If yes it is not Critical; file it
as "primitive present" at a lower severity. (5) Has the program rejected this severity class before?
items.how:
In this domain the gates that most often survive and kill a Critical are: the handshake
identifier in D05-052; the UID-scoped `DownloadManager.query` in D05-023; the BAL visible-window
requirement on API 34+ in D05-051; and server-side re-assertion of entitlement in D05-015. Test each
explicitly before writing the title.
items.proof:
Two independent end-to-end reproductions, and the gate question answered in writing for each.
For a High or Critical, reproduce through two independent paths where possible — the shell path and the
attacker-APK path are genuinely different stacks.
items.escalation: n/a — this is a kill gate.
items.ruled_out_when:
n/a. If a claimed finding fails reproduction, do not silently drop it: record it in a
retraction appendix with the original signal and the disproving evidence. The inverse also holds — **do
not retract a confirmed finding that stopped reproducing because the client shipped a patch mid-engagement.**
Keep timestamped pre-patch evidence (the APK hash, the logcat, the video) and say so.

items.title: The five-screenshot pattern for a receiver state-change finding
items.vrt: n/a — evidence standard
items.applies_to: Every D05 finding whose impact is a state change (D05-014, -015, -016, -024).
items.maps_to: Evidence-hygiene five-screenshot pattern; PoC standard
items.test:
Shared doctrine with D04-065, D08-066 and D13-008; the D05-specific content is which five frames a receiver state change needs. A state change needs a pre-state, the bug, and a post-state — plus the out-of-band side effect.
For a receiver finding the five beats map as follows.
items.how:
1. **Pre-state:** `adb shell run-as com.target.app cat shared_prefs/config.xml` showing the original
   value, and the app's traffic going to the real host.
2. **The bug:** the broadcast being sent from the zero-permission PoC (its `requested permissions` block
   visible in the same frame), with the marker in the extra.
3. **Post-state negative:** the old value gone from the prefs XML.
4. **Post-state positive:** the marker value present, and the app's next authenticated request arriving at
   your host.
5. **Side effect:** whether the app or the backend raised any alert — proves whether a passive defence
   exists.
```
Filenames: {finding-#}-step{n}-{description}.png
e.g. 05-step2-broadcast-from-zeropermission-app.png
```
Take all five in one sitting; do not relaunch the app between them, because a relaunch re-reads config and
invalidates the earlier captures. Redact the token body; **leave visible** the JSON key names, the trace
or request ids, your own attacker package name and UID — the triager needs those to correlate with
server-side logs.
items.proof: Five numbered, cross-referenced images, referenced by filename in the report body.
items.escalation: n/a.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — this is a deliverable standard, not a test.

2. File the over-broad FileProvider root (D07) separately — it has an independent fix surface.

items.title: Receiver that calls `send()` on a caller-supplied `PendingIntent` — BAL donation, not redirection
items.severity_note: Medium standalone; High when the donated launch lands a UI redress or a locked-screen activity
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.privilege_escalation` (varies)
items.applies_to: Exported or runtime-exported receivers that read a `PendingIntent` extra and call `send()` on it.
items.maps_to: MASTG-KNOW-0024, MASTG-TEST-0381, MASTG-BEST-0063; `developer.android.com/guide/components/activities/background-starts` (PendingIntent sender opt-in, API 34)
items.record: logs/D05-065.txt (the `ActivityTaskManager` BAL lines and the probe `PROBE|picanary|…` lines); screenshots/D05-065-1.png (your activity resumed while backgrounded)
items.skip_when: `grep -rlE 'PendingIntent' $DEC/jadx/sources | xargs grep -lE 'extends BroadcastReceiver|onReceive\(' | wc -l` prints 0 — write `n/a — D05-065: no receiver reads a PendingIntent extra`.
items.test:
`PendingIntent.send()` executes with the **creator's** identity, so when the attacker supplies the
token the victim's UID is never borrowed — that is why the bare shape is P5, and why it is not D05-028
(nested-Intent redirection). What the victim does donate is its **visibility**: on API <= 33 a visible sender
implicitly allowed the creator to start an activity from the background; on API >= 34 only if the sender
opts in (`ActivityOptions.setPendingIntentBackgroundActivityStartMode(MODE_BACKGROUND_ACTIVITY_START_ALLOWED)`)
or targets < 34. Find the opt-in, or the legacy device, and the attacker gets a background activity launch at
a moment of the victim's choosing.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE '\(PendingIntent\) *[A-Za-z0-9_.]*(get|extras)|getParcelableExtra\([^)]*PendingIntent|PendingIntent\.class' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | grep -i receiver
grep -rnE 'setPendingIntentBackgroundActivityStartMode|MODE_BACKGROUND_ACTIVITY_START_ALLOWED|BackgroundActivityStartMode' "$DEC/jadx/sources"
# probe: hand the receiver a mutable PendingIntent to our LootActivity under the key the handler reads, move to the background, watch the BAL verdict
adb shell "am start -S -n com.sanehunters.probe/.MainActivity --es run picanary --es victim com.target.app --es component .TheReceiver --es action com.target.app.ACTION --es pikey pendingIntent"
adb logcat -s ActivityTaskManager PROBE | grep -E 'balAllowedByPiSender|resultIfPiSenderAllowsBal|realCallerStartMode|Background activity launch|PROBE\|loot'
```
On a userdebug image `adb shell am compat disable 244637991 com.target.app` restores the API <= 33 sender
semantics for a LEGACY control run; record the device API and the victim's targetSdk next to every verdict.
items.proof:
Your activity resuming while your app was in the background, with the `ActivityTaskManager` line
showing `balAllowedByPiSender=true` (or the legacy allow) attributed to the victim's UID, plus the probe's
`PROBE|loot|extra=probe_canary` line proving the victim sent it.
items.escalation:
→ D04 (UI redress / task hijack timed to the victim's screen); → D08 for the sender-side
PendingIntent audit; → D22 for the API-34 behaviour gate.
items.ruled_out_when:
The receiver calls `send()` with no fill-in Intent (the caller cannot add data, flags or
extras) **and** the device is API >= 34 **and** the victim targets >= 34 without the sender opt-in: then no
identity and no visibility is donated — record the shape as P5 with this sentence so it is not re-raised.

items.title: Protected-broadcast receiver reached by making the system send it
items.vrt: `broken_access_control.exposed_sensitive_android_intent` (varies)
items.applies_to: Receivers whose only filters are protected actions whose payload is derived from a third-party-controllable event (package install/removal, account add/removal, widget options).
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0366, MASWE-0018; `developer.android.com/reference/android/accounts/AccountManager` (`LOGIN_ACCOUNTS_CHANGED_ACTION`, `ACTION_ACCOUNT_REMOVED`, account visibility); `developer.android.com/reference/android/content/Intent` (`ACTION_PACKAGE_ADDED/REMOVED/FULLY_REMOVED`, `EXTRA_UID`)
items.record: logs/D05-066.txt (the handler's side effect and the `BroadcastQueue` delivery line per route); pocs/F-NNN/ with the probe manifest when it became a finding
items.skip_when: `grep -cE 'PACKAGE_(ADDED|REPLACED|REMOVED|FULLY_REMOVED)|LOGIN_ACCOUNTS_CHANGED|ACCOUNT_REMOVED|APPWIDGET_UPDATE_OPTIONS' $DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml` and the same grep over `$DEC/jadx/sources` both print 0 — write `n/a — D05-066: no receiver consumes a package, account or widget-options broadcast`.
items.test:
You cannot forge the action (D05-005/006), but you can often **cause** it with a payload you chose.
(1) `PACKAGE_ADDED/REPLACED/REMOVED`: install or remove an app whose **package name you choose** — the
handler receives `package:<yourname>` in `getData()` and `EXTRA_UID`; look for handlers that pattern-match
the name (companion/plugin/sibling detection) or splice it into a path, URL or SQL. (2)
`LOGIN_ACCOUNTS_CHANGED` / `ACTION_ACCOUNT_REMOVED`: ship an authenticator for an account type the handler
reacts to (or the victim's own type if unguarded — see D03-043) and add/remove an account; the handler
receives an attacker-chosen account name and type. (3) `APPWIDGET_UPDATE_OPTIONS`: a zero-permission
`AppWidgetHost` (one bind-confirmation tap) calls `updateAppWidgetOptions` and the system delivers your
options Bundle to the provider.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'PACKAGE_(ADDED|REPLACED|REMOVED|FULLY_REMOVED)|LOGIN_ACCOUNTS_CHANGED|ACCOUNT_REMOVED|APPWIDGET_UPDATE_OPTIONS' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml" "$DEC/jadx/sources"
grep -rnE 'getSchemeSpecificPart\(\)|EXTRA_UID|KEY_ACCOUNT_NAME|KEY_ACCOUNT_TYPE|getAppWidgetOptions' "$DEC/jadx/sources" | grep -i receiver -A6
# (1) choose the package name the handler matches, build the probe under that name, then:
adb install "$E/pocs/D05-066/probe-<chosen.package.name>.apk"; adb uninstall <chosen.package.name>
adb logcat -s BroadcastQueue | grep -E 'com.target.app'     # the delivery line for the victim is the control that the system sent it
```
For (2) on API >= 26 the system delivers account broadcasts only to packages the account is **visible** to:
your authenticator must call `setAccountVisibility(account, "com.target.app", VISIBILITY_VISIBLE)` **and**
declare `<queries><package android:name="com.target.app"/></queries>`, or the system silently withholds the
broadcast and your negative is a visibility artefact, not a control.
items.proof:
The handler's side effect (marker in prefs, log or a request, D05-010) following a system-sent
protected broadcast whose payload you chose, from a probe declaring no permissions.
items.escalation: Whatever the handler does — D05-014/015/016; account handlers → D13.
items.ruled_out_when:
The handler validates the package or account against a signature or a server-issued
list before acting, or you proved the broadcast was delivered (the `BroadcastQueue` line for the victim) and
the handler no-op'd — quote the check. A missing delivery with no `<queries>`/visibility grant on your side
is untested, not negative.
